summary: Defines an option for negotiating header compression on IP datagrams over the Point-to-Point Protocol, by extending the PPP control protocols for IPv4 and IPv6. Compression can apply to IP headers combined with TCP, UDP, and RTP. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: IP header compression works by sending a short number that stands for a whole packet header, and by sending the full header occasionally so the other end can keep up. Before any of that can happen, the two ends of a PPP link have to agree on the rules: how many such numbers are available, how often a full header has to be sent, and how large a header may be. This document defines that agreement, and the packet types the link uses to carry the different kinds of compressed header.

questions: what is ip header compression over ppp
what is the ppp ip-compression-protocol option
how does ppp negotiate header compression
subtitle: How a PPP link negotiates IP header compression, and the nine packet types the link has to tell apart.

tldr.problem: On a slow link, a large part of every packet is a header that repeats what the previous packet already said, and a PPP link needs a way to agree with the other end on how to compress those headers and how to undo that.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines a configuration option for the IP control protocol and the IPv6 control protocol, with fields for the context identifier spaces, the interval between full headers and the largest header that may be compressed, plus suboptions that turn on RTP compression or restrict compression to one kind of traffic.
tldr.outcome: Nine new values for the PPP data link layer protocol field let the two ends tell the compressed header formats apart, including the formats for UDP and RTP. The document obsoletes RFC 2509 and adds two suboptions to it.

today: RFC 3544 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2003 and has not been obsoleted. It obsoleted RFC 2509, adding two suboptions to the compression option: one for the enhanced RTP compression of RFC 3545, and one that lets an end negotiate compression for TCP only or for non-TCP only. The compression scheme itself is specified in RFC 2507 and RFC 2508.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
To establish compression of IP datagrams sent over a PPP link, each end of the link must agree on a set of configuration parameters for the compression. Negotiating link parameters for network layer protocols is handled in PPP by a family of network control protocols. Since there are separate control protocols for IPv4 and IPv6, this document defines configuration options to be used in both of them to negotiate parameters for the compression scheme.

The document obsoletes RFC 2509 and adds two new suboptions to the IP header compression configuration option. One suboption negotiates the use of enhanced RTP compression, and the other negotiates header compression for only TCP or only non-TCP packets.

IP header compression relies on the link layer's ability to indicate the types of datagrams carried in its frames, and this document defines nine new types for the PPP Data Link Layer Protocol Field along with their meaning.

In general, header compression schemes that use delta encoding of compressed packets require that the lower layer does not reorder packets between the compressor and the decompressor. IP header compression uses delta encoding of compressed packets for TCP and RTP, and the compression specification includes methods that allow link layers that may reorder packets to be used with it. Since PPP does not reorder packets, those mechanisms are disabled by default. When using reordering mechanisms such as multiclass multilink PPP, care must be taken so that packets that share the same compression context are not reordered.
sections.plainLanguage: Compression here is not a new idea: it is a scheme defined elsewhere, and this document is about the PPP-specific parts. Those are the option that negotiates it and the packet types the link carries, because the link has to say which kind of compressed header each frame holds.

sections.title: The Configuration Option
sections.content:
The document specifies a new compression protocol value for the IP-Compression-Protocol option of the IP control protocol, and describes the associated option format. The option format is structured to allow future extensions to the compression scheme.

Both the IPv4 control protocol and the IPv6 control protocol may be used to negotiate IP header compression parameters for their respective protocols, and the format of the configuration option is the same for both. Successful negotiation enables the use of the protocol identifiers FULL_HEADER, COMPRESSED_TCP, COMPRESSED_TCP_NODELTA, COMPRESSED_NON_TCP and CONTEXT_STATE.

The option has a type field of 2, a length of 14 octets or more, which may be increased when additional parameters are indicated by additional suboptions, and the IP-Compression-Protocol value 0061 in hexadecimal. It then carries four parameter fields and a list of suboptions.

TCP_SPACE is two octets and gives the maximum value of a context identifier in the space allocated for TCP. The suggested value is 15, and it must be at least 0 and at most 255, where a value of 0 implies having one context. NON_TCP_SPACE is two octets and gives the maximum value of a context identifier in the space allocated for non-TCP; these identifiers are carried in the COMPRESSED_NON_TCP, COMPRESSED_UDP and COMPRESSED_RTP packet headers. The suggested value is 15, and it must be at least 0 and at most 65535, where 0 again implies one context.

F_MAX_PERIOD is the maximum interval between full headers: no more than F_MAX_PERIOD COMPRESSED_NON_TCP headers may be sent between FULL_HEADER headers. The suggested value is 256, and a value of zero means infinity, with no limit on the number of consecutive compressed headers. F_MAX_TIME is the maximum time interval between full headers, so that compressed headers may not be sent more than F_MAX_TIME seconds after the last full header. The suggested value is 5 seconds, and zero again means infinity. MAX_HEADER is the largest header size in octets that may be compressed, with a suggested value of 168 octets. It should be large enough that at least the outer network layer header can be compressed, and to increase compression efficiency it should cover common combinations of network and transport layer headers.

The suboptions field holds zero or more suboptions, each of a type field, a length field and zero or more parameter octets, where the length includes the type and length fields themselves. The document notes that the PPP specification does not prohibit several instances of one configuration option unless the option's own specification says so, and that RFC 3241 updates the IPv4 control protocol to allow the sending of multiple instances of the IP-Compression-Protocol option with different values, so that each type of compression protocol can establish its own parameters. It also assumes, in line with current practice, that the option describes the capabilities of the decompressor of the peer that sends the configuration request.
sections.plainLanguage: The option has a fixed part of 14 bytes and then a list of suboptions. The fixed part says how many short identifiers are available for TCP and for everything else, how many compressed packets may be sent before a full header has to be sent again, how long that may take, and how large a header may be before it is too big to compress.

sections.title: The Suboptions
sections.content:
The RTP-Compression suboption is included in the compression option when IP, UDP and RTP compression is to be enabled. Including it enables the use of the protocol identifiers COMPRESSED_RTP and COMPRESSED_UDP, along with additional forms of CONTEXT_STATE. Its type is 1 and its length is 2.

The Enhanced RTP-Compression suboption has type 2 and length 2, and is used to enable the enhanced RTP header compression defined in RFC 3545. It enables the protocol identifiers COMPRESSED_RTP and CONTEXT_STATE, and in addition enables compression compliant with RFC 3545, including the use of the COMPRESSED_UDP protocol identifier with additional flags, and the use of the C flag with the FULL_HEADER protocol identifier to indicate the use of the header checksum with COMPRESSED_RTP and COMPRESSED_UDP packets. Sub-option 2 is negotiated instead of, not in addition to, sub-option 1.

The third suboption, with type 3 and length 3, allows header compression to be negotiated for only TCP or only non-TCP packets. It exists because in RFC 2509 it was not possible to negotiate only TCP header compression or only non-TCP header compression, since a value of 0 in the TCP_SPACE or NON_TCP_SPACE field actually means that one context is negotiated. The new suboption has a one-byte parameter: 1 sets the number of contexts for TCP_SPACE to 0, and 2 sets the number of contexts for NON_TCP_SPACE to 0. It overrides the values previously assigned to those fields in the compression option. If suboption 3 is included several times with parameter 1 and 2, compression is disabled for all packets.
sections.plainLanguage: Three suboptions tune the scheme. One turns on compression for RTP and UDP traffic. Another turns on the newer, enhanced version of RTP compression, and replaces the first rather than adding to it. The third is for turning compression off for one kind of traffic, which the old fields could not express because a zero there meant one context rather than none.

sections.title: Multiple Network Control Protocols
sections.content:
The compression scheme is able to compress both IPv6 and IPv4 datagrams, and both the IPv4 and the IPv6 control protocols are able to negotiate option parameter values for it. Those values apply to the compression of packets whose outer header is an IPv4 header and an IPv6 header respectively.

For the compression and decompression of IPv4 and IPv6 datagram headers the context identifier space is shared. While the parameter values are negotiated independently, sharing the identifier spaces becomes more complex when the values differ. Since the compressed packets share the identifier space, the compression engine must allocate identifiers out of a common pool, and for compressed packets the decompressor has to examine the context state to determine what parameters to use for decompression.

Context identifier spaces are not shared between TCP and the non-TCP, UDP and RTP traffic. Doing so would need extra mechanisms to make sure that no error can occur when switching from using an identifier for TCP to non-TCP.
sections.plainLanguage: IPv4 and IPv6 share one pool of short identifiers, because a compressed packet does not say which version of IP it carries. TCP and the other protocols get separate pools, so that the decompressor can tell from the identifier alone which kind of header it stands for.

sections.title: Demultiplexing of Datagrams
sections.content:
The IP header compression specification defines four header formats for different types of compressed header: compressed TCP, compressed TCP with no delta encoding, compressed non-TCP with an 8-bit context identifier, and compressed non-TCP with a 16-bit context identifier. The two non-TCP formats may be distinguished by their contents, so both may use the same link-level identifier. A fifth format, the full header, is distinct in that it carries the additional information that establishes the shared context between the compressor and the decompressor.

The IP/UDP/RTP header compression specification defines four further formats: compressed UDP and compressed RTP on top of UDP, both with either 8-bit or 16-bit context identifiers, and an explicit error message from the decompressor to the compressor. The link layer must be able to indicate these formats with distinct values, and nine PPP Data Link Layer Protocol Field values are specified.

FULL_HEADER, value 0061 in hexadecimal, carries a full header as specified in the IP/UDP/RTP header compression document, which is the same as the full header in the IP header compression specification. COMPRESSED_TCP, value 0063, carries a datagram with a compressed header in the format of Section 6a of that specification. COMPRESSED_TCP_NODELTA, value 2063, carries a datagram with a compressed header in the format of Section 6b. COMPRESSED_NON_TCP, value 0065, carries a datagram with a compressed header in either the format of Section 6c or that of Section 6d.

COMPRESSED_RTP_8, value 0069, and COMPRESSED_RTP_16, value 2069, carry compressed RTP headers with 8-bit and 16-bit context identifiers. COMPRESSED_UDP_8, value 0067, and COMPRESSED_UDP_16, value 2067, carry compressed UDP headers with 8-bit and 16-bit context identifiers. CONTEXT_STATE, value 2065, is a link-level message sent from the decompressor to the compressor.
sections.plainLanguage: The link has to distinguish nine kinds of frame: a full header, three kinds of compressed TCP header, one kind of compressed header for everything else, and the compressed UDP and RTP headers in their 8-bit and 16-bit forms, plus a message the decompressor sends back to the compressor. Each has its own value in the PPP protocol field.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 2509
sections.content: Two new suboptions are specified, in Sections 2.3 and 2.4: the enhanced RTP compression suboption, which enables the compression of RFC 3545, and the suboption that negotiates header compression for only TCP or only non-TCP packets.
sections.plainLanguage: Two things were added to what RFC 2509 had: a switch to the newer RTP compression, and the ability to compress only one kind of traffic.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Negotiation of the option defined here imposes no additional security considerations beyond those that otherwise apply to PPP.

The use of header compression can, in rare cases, cause the misdelivery of packets. If necessary, confidentiality of packet contents should be assured by encryption.

Encryption applied at the IP layer, for example using IPsec mechanisms, precludes header compression of the encrypted headers, though compression of the outer IP header and the authentication and security headers is still possible. For RTP packets, full header compression is possible if the RTP payload is encrypted by itself without encrypting the UDP or RTP headers. That method is appropriate when the UDP and RTP header information does not need to be kept confidential.
sections.plainLanguage: Negotiating the option adds no security of its own. The one risk to be aware of is that compression can, rarely, deliver a packet to the wrong place, so anything that must stay secret should be encrypted. Encrypting at the IP layer means the encrypted headers cannot be compressed, though the outer header still can.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: 14 or more, when suboptions are present.

fields.name: IP-Compression-Protocol
fields.desc: 0061 in hexadecimal, the IP header compression protocol.

fields.name: TCP_SPACE
fields.desc: The highest context identifier in the space allocated for TCP. Suggested value 15.

fields.name: NON_TCP_SPACE
fields.desc: The highest context identifier in the space allocated for non-TCP. Suggested value 15.

fields.name: F_MAX_PERIOD
fields.desc: The most compressed non-TCP headers between full headers. Suggested value 256; zero means no limit.

fields.name: F_MAX_TIME
fields.desc: The longest gap between full headers, in seconds. Suggested value 5; zero means no limit.

fields.name: MAX_HEADER
fields.desc: The largest header that may be compressed, in octets. Suggested value 168.

items.text: Type 1 for RTP compression, type 2 for enhanced RTP compression, type 3 to turn off TCP or non-TCP compression.

viz.caption: THE NINE PPP PROTOCOL FIELD VALUES

items.label: FULL_HEADER
items.desc: A full header, carrying the information that establishes the shared context.

items.label: COMPRESSED_TCP

items.label: COMPRESSED_TCP_NODELTA
items.desc: A compressed TCP header without delta encoding.

items.label: COMPRESSED_NON_TCP
items.desc: A compressed non-TCP header, with an 8 or 16 bit context identifier.

items.desc: A compressed RTP header with 8-bit context identifiers.

items.label: COMPRESSED_RTP_16
items.desc: A compressed RTP header with 16-bit context identifiers.

items.desc: A compressed UDP header with 8-bit context identifiers.

items.label: COMPRESSED_UDP_16
items.desc: A compressed UDP header with 16-bit context identifiers.

items.desc: A link-level message from the decompressor to the compressor.
